To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
undernutrition of rats during their suckling period produces a deficit of glycerophoshatidylcholine in white matter but spares glycerophosphatidylethanoamine.
moderate and severe undernutrition of the rat during suckling produces deficits in the activities of the synthetic enzymes for glycerophosphatides in white matter but no deficits for gray matter.
undernutrition during the sucklingperiod produces deficits in the glycerophopholipid content in white matter but no deficits in the glyerophospholipd content of gray matter.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the synthesis of phospholipids by the brain and their metabolism in vivo.
the effect of early undernutrition on the brain of rats, and we are particularly interested in how the synthesis of phospholipids is affected.
the effects of undernutrition of the rat during the suckling and weaning period on the synthesis of glycerophopholipids.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the effects of undernutrition on the synthesis of glycerophosholipids are not the same in white matter as in gray matter, and the effects on the synthetic enzyme activities are not the same for phosphoethano-lamine transferase as for phosphocholine tranferase.
the effects of undernutrition on the synthesis of glyceropholipids in the brain of rats is complex and not readily explained by changes in enzyme activities.
the undernutrition‐induced deficits in glycerophosphoglycolipid content of white matter are due to a decreased synthesis of glycerophoshatidylethanolamines and phosphatidyl‐serines.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
phospholipids are spared in gray matter and reduced in white matter during the suckling phase of brain development.
the deficits in phospholipid content in the brain of undernourished animals are due to a reduction of phospholipid synthetic capacity.
undernutrition during the suckling stage produces deficits of glycolipids and phosphoglycerides in white matter but only deficits of phosphoglycerides, and no glycolipids, in gray matter.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain is able to compensate for the loss of phospholipids in the gray matter.
the brain is a dynamic organ that is constantly adapting and responding to its environment.
